唐纳德·特朗普规模庞大、推进迅速的美国 AI 建设计划如今面临重大放缓：在昨天的选举中，选民以压倒性多数支持了主张在全国范围内加强对 AI 和数据中心限制的候选人和议案。

inlines.text: 唐纳德·特朗普规模庞大、推进迅速的美国 AI 建设计划如今面临重大放缓：在昨天的选举中，选民以压倒性多数支持了主张在全国范围内加强对 AI 和数据中心限制的候选人和议案。

blocks.text: 一家名为 Redbud Consulting 的民调公司追踪了选票上的数据中心相关议案，报告称在 10 个州提出的 44 项旨在限制数据中心的议案中，目前已有 38 项获得通过。这些议案包括数十项暂停令和禁令。分析人士认为，这些措施不会影响已经开工或已获批、将于 2027 年前建成的数据中心，主要影响的是计划于 2028 年推进的未来项目。只有一项议案获得通过，允许一个数据中心继续推进。但即便是这一小小的胜利，也代表着对 AI 行业的抵制——它要求北达科他州某市的数据中心开发商在扩建或提出项目时，出资进行独立审查并举行公开听证会。

blocks.text: 除了加强对数据中心的监管，选民们还支持反AI的候选人，在那些正在美国建设最多数据中心容量的关键州，选出了誓言要严厉打击的官员。

blocks.text: 最引人注目的是，民主党挑战者Gina Hinojosa赢得了得克萨斯州州长竞选，Axios报道称，这将从根本上打乱特朗普AI建设计划的算盘。据彭博社报道，Hinojosa的当选让开发商面临“最坏情况”。Axios指出，得州是AI热潮的中心，预计到2028年将占新增数据中心容量的41%以上。

blocks.text: 如今，Hinojosa计划推迟项目，直到通过法律“解决对水、电、空气和产权的影响”为止。彭博社报道，目前约有“13吉瓦的数据中心容量”受到影响。据彭博社报道，GLJ Research的Gordon Johnson在一份报告中警告，得州那些“电力、许可和钢材都已到位”的项目会继续推进，但“有电力却没有州环境许可的项目将推迟12到18个月”。一些项目可能完全离开该州，或许迁往路易斯安那州或佐治亚州——也可能哪儿都去不了。

inlines.text: 大型科技公司淡化AI选举结果

blocks.text: 得州并非唯一的大变动。民主党还赢下了另外三个此前招揽数据中心开发商的大州——亚利桑那州、佐治亚州和俄亥俄州——的州长选举。总体而言，Axios预测，“2028年近三分之二的数据中心容量”可能面临与Hinojosa在得州所威胁的类似延迟。彭博社估计，美国一半的数据中心现在更容易受到审查。

inlines.text: 得州并非唯一的大变动。民主党还赢下了另外三个此前招揽数据中心开发商的大州——亚利桑那州、佐治亚州和俄亥俄州——的州长选举。总体而言，Axios预测，“2028年近三分之二的数据中心容量”可能面临与Hinojosa在得州所威胁的类似延迟。彭博社估计，美国一半的数据中心现在更容易受到审查。

blocks.text: 对AI公司来说，这是一场噩梦，因为任何延迟都会拖累收入，而IT咨询公司Gartner最近估计，“AI热潮距离收回成本还差近5万亿美元。”

blocks.text: 尽管许多报道认为，首场所谓的“AI选举”证明了人民约束大型科技公司的力量，但一些AI行业内部人士周三淡化了选举结果。Adam Kovacevich——前谷歌高管、科技行业贸易团体兼政策联盟Chamber of Progress的首席执行官——在一份声明中表示，“选举结果几乎没有证据表明选民授权打击AI或数据中心。”他强调，“反对数据中心禁令的民主党州长候选人胜选率高于支持禁令的候选人”，并告诫说，“不要把反特朗普浪潮与反科技授权混为一谈。”

inlines.text: 民调：四分之三选民反对数据中心

blocks.text: NBC新闻的出口民调显示，生活成本或政府腐败等问题在选民心中的重要性确实高于AI和数据中心。然而，与许多把反对AI视为选民关键决定因素的分析人士一样，民权与技术领导会议中心副主席亚历杭德拉·蒙托亚-博耶并不认同科瓦切维奇的视角。

inlines.text: 显示，生活成本或政府腐败等问题在选民心中的重要性确实高于AI和数据中心。然而，与许多把反对AI视为选民关键决定因素的分析人士一样，民权与技术领导会议中心副主席亚历杭德拉·蒙托亚-博耶并不认同科瓦切维奇的视角。

blocks.text: “2026年中期选举是美国第一场真正意义上的AI选举，”蒙托亚-博耶说。“我们看到选民以创纪录的中期选举投票率前往投票站，把票投给那些愿意保护他们及其权利、使其免受不受约束的AI侵害的领导人。”

inlines.text: “2026年中期选举是美国第一场真正意义上的AI选举，”蒙托亚-博耶说。“我们看到选民以创纪录的中期选举投票率前往投票站，把票投给那些愿意保护他们及其权利、使其免受不受约束的AI侵害的领导人。”

blocks.text: 蒙托亚-博耶援引NBC的民调称，四分之三的选民反对数据中心。此外，超过半数选民表示，“AI和数据中心是他们投票选举国会议员的关键或重要因素”。蒙托亚-博耶认为，这种大规模反弹不仅关乎电费或其他对数据中心的担忧，更源于选民不信任共和党能监管好AI。蒙托亚-博耶说，选举日到来之际，“最大的AI公司正竞相上市，AI系统冲破了本应用来约束它们的测试‘沙盒’，带有偏见和歧视的AI不断对我们做出改变人生的决定。”

inlines.text: 周三，特朗普在 Truth Social 上连发多条帖子回应选举结果，却只字未提 AI。他似乎把矛头指向福克斯新闻，怪它给民主党人提供平台，同时声称如果自己出现在选票上，结果会有所不同。

blocks.text: 但特朗普的沉默表明，他没有什么谈话要点可以掩饰这一事实：Blue Rose Research 的民调显示，“美国人宁愿住在监狱、美沙酮诊所或核电站附近，也不愿住在 AI 数据中心附近。”而尽管像 Anthropic 这样的 AI 公司最近警告的存在性担忧让许多美国人感到不安，但 Blue Rose 的研究总监 Ali Mortell 对《时代》表示，对选民而言，“具体的本地影响”如更高的能源账单或污染“要显著得多”。即便开发商承诺承担成本，“对机构的信任也很低”，以至于 Mortell 说，即使“当科技公司和政客提供保证时”，“选民也不认为那是真的。”

Voters seize their moment to slow down Trump’s rapid AI buildout

inlines.text: Voters seize their moment to slow down Trump’s rapid AI buildout

blocks.text: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.

Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

inlines.text: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

blocks.text: One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.

blocks.text: In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.

inlines.text: In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.

blocks.text: Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg, Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.

blocks.text: Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.

blocks.text: Big Tech downplays AI election results

inlines.text: Big Tech downplays AI election results

blocks.text: Texas wasn’t the only big shake-up. Democrats won governor races in the next three biggest states previously wooing data center developers—Arizona, Georgia, and Ohio. Overall, Axios projected that “nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity” could face similar delays as Hinojosa threatens in Texas. Bloomberg estimated that half the data centers in the US are now more vulnerable to scrutiny.

blocks.text: While many reports suggested that the first so-called “AI election” proved the power of the people to rein in Big Tech, some AI industry insiders downplayed the election results on Wednesday. In a statement, Adam Kovacevich—a former Google executive and the CEO of a tech industry trade group and policy coalition called Chamber of Progress—suggested “the results offer little evidence of a voter mandate to crack down on AI or data centers.” He emphasized that “Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data center bans won at a higher rate than those who supported them,” and admonished, “Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate.”

blocks.text: “Voters wanted change on the economy, not a crackdown on innovation,” Kovacevich said, while sharing a resource for those in the tech industry seeking an alternative spin on the results.

blocks.text: NBC News exit polls suggest it’s true that issues like cost of living or government corruption were ranked as more significant by voters than AI and data centers. However, like many analysts who point to AI opposition as a make-or-break issue for many voters, Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, vice president of The Leadership Conference’s Center for Civil Rights and Technology, disagreed with Kovacevich’s lens.

blocks.text: “The 2026 midterms have been the first true AI election in the US,” Montoya-Boyer said. “We saw voters turn up at the polls in record midterm numbers and vote for leaders who are willing to protect them and their rights from unchecked AI.”

inlines.text: “The 2026 midterms have been the first true AI election in the US,” Montoya-Boyer said. “We saw voters turn up at the polls in record midterm numbers and vote for leaders who are willing to protect them and their rights from unchecked AI.”

blocks.text: Montoya-Boyer cited NBC’s polls showing that 3 in 4 voters are opposed to data centers. Additionally, more than half of voters said that “AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.” The mass backlash is not just about utility costs or other data center fears, Montoya-Boyer suggested, but instead stemmed from distrust in Republicans to regulate AI. Election day came “as the biggest AI companies raced to go public, AI systems broke out of the test ‘sandboxes’ meant to contain them, and biased and discriminatory AI kept making life-altering decisions about us,” Montoya-Boyer said.

blocks.text: Other analysts told Axios that voters appeared to be “more concerned about efforts to block state AI regulation than they are about data center controversies,” with one noting that across four swing districts, “voters trust Democrats over Republicans to hold AI executives accountable by a margin of 7 to 10 points.” Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios that “voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers.”
